While there's a brief physical altercation at the concert ("Get off my stage.", "They throwin' garbage?", "Abdul assaulted me!"), it doesn't fundamentally alter the narrative's trajectory. The challenges they face are mostly resolved through comedic antics and social manipulation, not physical force. The threat of violence from Paula Abdul is present, but it's played for comedic effect and ultimately resolved through forgiveness, not further violence. The narrative focuses on friendship and comedic mishaps, with force playing a very minor role.

title: I Still Believe
justification: The film's narrative focuses on themes of faith, love, loss, and grief, with minimal emphasis on force or violence as a means of resolving conflict. The central conflict revolves around Melissa's battle with cancer and Jeremy's emotional and spiritual journey. While there are moments of emotional intensity and internal struggle, the characters primarily rely on faith, prayer, and mutual support to navigate their challenges. The dialogue emphasizes themes of hope, resilience, and the power of belief in the face of adversity, rather than advocating for or depicting violent solutions.

title: Emma.
justification: The subtitles of "Emma" contain virtually no instances of force or violence being used to resolve conflict. The narrative revolves around social interactions, matchmaking, and personal growth, with dialogue focused on relationships, manners, and societal expectations. The closest instance is a brief mention of gypsies attacking Harriet, but this is quickly resolved without any violent retaliation. The narrative emphasizes dialogue, social maneuvering, and emotional intelligence as the primary means of navigating conflicts and achieving resolution, rather than physical force.

title: Come Play
justification: While the film primarily focuses on themes of loneliness, communication, and family, force/violence appears in a limited capacity. Byron is physically injured, seemingly by Larry, leading to accusations against Oliver: "It was... it was Oliver. He's a freak." This incident escalates the conflict and briefly positions violence as a potential outcome of Oliver's perceived otherness. However, the narrative ultimately refutes this, revealing Larry as the true source of the harm and shifting the focus towards understanding and empathy. The resolution hinges on emotional connection and acceptance rather than physical confrontation, diminishing the overall salience of force as a problem-solving method.

title: Let Him Go
justification: Force/violence is the dominant engine of resolution in this film. The narrative escalates from subtle intimidation to outright violence, with characters consistently resorting to physical coercion to achieve their goals. Blanche Weboy and her sons use threats and physical force to maintain control over Lorna and Jimmy, culminating in a brutal confrontation. George and Margaret's attempts to rescue Jimmy are met with escalating violence, including George's hand being mutilated. The climax involves a deadly shootout and arson, underscoring the film's reliance on force as the primary means of resolving conflict, and ultimately, George sacrifices himself in a final act of violent resistance.

title: Freaky
justification: Force/violence is central to the narrative's resolution. The Blissfield Butcher's murders instigate the plot, and the characters' survival depends on their ability to fight back. Millie and the Butcher swap bodies after being stabbed with La Dola, an ancient Aztecan dagger used in ritual sacrifice. The narrative progresses as Millie and her friends attempt to reverse the body swap by stabbing the Butcher with the dagger before midnight, leading to multiple violent confrontations. The climax involves a final showdown at the homecoming dance, where Millie and her friends must use force to stop the Butcher from killing more people and to restore Millie to her own body.

title: Downhill
justification: The subtitles contain no instances of characters using or planning violence to resolve disputes. The narrative focuses on interpersonal conflicts and emotional resolutions, rather than physical force. The closest instance is when Pete almost collides with his son on the ski slope, but this is an accident and not an intentional act of aggression. The narrative primarily revolves around communication, emotional processing, and personal growth, making force/violence a non-salient theme.

title: Cats
justification: Force and violence are moderately central to the narrative. Macavity uses coercion and physical threat to attempt to win the Jellicle Choice, such as when he chains up Bustopher Jones and threatens Old Deuteronomy. Growltiger acts as Macavity's enforcer, physically restraining other cats. While magic and talent are presented as ways to succeed, Macavity's violent actions create significant conflict and drive the plot, even though ultimately unsuccessful. The narrative also features the antics of Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer, who engage in disruptive and destructive behavior, though it is more mischievous than overtly violent.

title: It's a Wonderful Life
justification: The film "It's a Wonderful Life" primarily focuses on themes of community, sacrifice, and the value of life, with minimal emphasis on force or violence as a means of resolving conflict. The narrative revolves around George Bailey's emotional struggles and his eventual realization of the positive impact he has had on his community. While there are instances of conflict, such as George's arguments with Mr. Potter, these are resolved through dialogue and the support of the community, rather than through physical force. The film's climax involves a community coming together to financially support George, highlighting the power of collective support rather than individual force.

title: The Hunt
justification: Force/violence is the dominant engine of resolution in this film. The central premise involves kidnapping individuals and hunting them for sport, immediately establishing violence as a core element. Characters are given weapons and forced to fight for survival, as seen when Lou says, "What do we need guns for? We'll get out of here." The narrative progresses through numerous violent encounters, including shootings, explosions, and hand-to-hand combat, with characters frequently resorting to lethal force to overcome obstacles and enemies. The climax involves a final, brutal confrontation where the protagonist uses violence to defeat the antagonist, Athena, solidifying force as the primary means of resolving the conflict.

title: The Rhythm Section
justification: The subtitles depict a scenario where violence, specifically a bomb, is central to the narrative. The dialogue includes explicit mentions of a bomb and a detonator, indicating a planned violent act. The urgency in the characters' voices, such as "Everyone get out!!" and "There's a bomb!", highlights the immediate threat of violence. The failure of the detonator and the revelation of a timer further emphasize the reliance on explosive force as a means to achieve a goal. The presence of a 'coward' suggests a betrayal or failure to execute the violent plan, which is still central to the plot.

title: The SpongeBob Movie: Sponge on the Run
justification: While the film primarily focuses on friendship and courage, force and coercion appear intermittently as methods for resolving conflict. King Poseidon initially uses his power to seize Gary and threatens SpongeBob and Patrick with execution. Plankton's schemes to steal the Krabby Patty formula, though comedic, involve coercion and the potential for harm. The zombie pirates in 'Goner Gulch' present a violent threat that SpongeBob and Patrick must overcome, albeit through unconventional means. However, these instances are balanced by the film's emphasis on non-violent solutions, such as friendship and understanding, ultimately reducing the overall salience of force as the primary means of resolution.

title: Richard Jewell
justification: While the film does not explicitly endorse violence as the primary solution, the narrative revolves around a bombing and its aftermath, where law enforcement and investigation are central. The protagonist, Richard Jewell, aspires to be in law enforcement and believes in protecting people, indicating a reliance on force and authority. However, the film primarily focuses on the investigation and legal processes following the bombing, rather than direct acts of violence. The dialogue includes threats and aggressive language, such as "I'm gonna bury you, you motherfucker," but these are not central to resolving the core conflict of Jewell's wrongful accusation.

title: The Broken Hearts Gallery
justification: The subtitles primarily focus on romantic relationships, breakups, and emotional healing. There are a few instances where characters express anger or frustration, such as Amanda's destructive outburst in Lucy's room and the brief physical altercation outside the restaurant. However, these moments are not central to resolving the main conflicts. The narrative emphasizes emotional processing, communication, and personal growth as ways to overcome challenges, rather than relying on force or violence. The focus remains on navigating relationships and finding personal fulfillment, with minimal reliance on physical aggression.

title: Infidel
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's core conflict. The film depicts Doug's kidnapping and imprisonment, where he faces physical and psychological torture to force a confession. The narrative escalates to a prison break orchestrated by Mossad, involving armed conflict and violence to extract Doug and other prisoners. The dialogue explicitly highlights the use of force, such as threats of violence to obtain Doug's blog password and the violent actions of various factions. The climax involves a shootout and escape, underscoring that survival and resolution depend on the capacity to use force.

title: News of the World
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in "News of the World." The narrative repeatedly presents situations where characters resort to violence or the threat of violence to achieve their goals. Captain Kidd and Johanna are threatened by Almay and his associates, leading to a violent confrontation where Kidd must use his skills to survive and protect Johanna. Later, Kidd and Johanna are confronted by Farley and his men, who use coercion and violence to control the town, culminating in a shootout. These instances demonstrate that force is a primary means of navigating the dangers and injustices present in the film's world, making it a central theme.

title: Bill & Ted Face the Music
justification: The film "Bill & Ted Face the Music" primarily focuses on the power of music and unity to solve problems, rather than force or violence. While there are instances of conflict and potential violence, such as the killer robot sent from the future and the older versions of Bill and Ted threatening their younger selves with guns, these are not central to the resolution of the main narrative. The film emphasizes collaboration, understanding, and the unifying power of music as the means to save reality. The characters ultimately resolve their issues through communication and cooperation, rather than resorting to physical force. The narrative arc revolves around creating a song that unites the world, not defeating enemies through violence.

title: The Empty Man
justification: Force and violence are central to the resolution of the narrative. The film revolves around a series of increasingly violent events and deaths linked to the "Empty Man" phenomenon. The protagonist, James, a former cop, resorts to physical coercion and threats to extract information, such as when he intimidates Davara to get into his car and later assaults the man in the hospital parking lot. The narrative culminates in the revelation that James himself is a construct created by a cult, designed to be a vessel for a destructive entity, and the only way to stop the entity is to eliminate James, which is achieved through violence.

title: My Boyfriend’s Meds
justification: The subtitles primarily focus on interpersonal relationships, romantic entanglements, and workplace dynamics. There is a brief moment where a drone goes "crazy" and Elliot is asked to stop it, but this is a minor event. The narrative revolves around communication, honesty, and personal growth, particularly concerning Hank's mental health and his relationships. The characters navigate their problems through dialogue and emotional expression, rather than resorting to physical force or violence. Therefore, force/violence is not structurally central to problem-solving in this narrative.

title: The Last Full Measure
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's core conflict. The film revolves around the actions of William Pitsenbarger, a pararescueman who repeatedly enters a violent combat zone to save soldiers. Dialogue such as "We're taking fire from all corners" and descriptions of the battle as an "ambush" highlight the pervasive violence. Characters like Billy Takoda, a "natural war fighter" who "loved it," exemplify the acceptance of violence. The narrative emphasizes that survival and justice in this context depend on the capacity to engage in combat, as seen in the numerous scenes of firefights and wounded soldiers.

title: Words on Bathroom Walls
justification: The subtitles contain minimal instances of force or violence being explicitly endorsed as a solution. The primary conflict revolves around Adam's mental health and his struggles with schizophrenia, rather than physical confrontations. While there is a scene where Adam gets into a fight with some guys from his old school, this is presented as a consequence of his past and not as a central method for resolving his problems. The focus remains on his internal struggles and relationships, with dialogue emphasizing understanding and support rather than aggression. The Bodyguard character is mentioned, suggesting a potential for physical intervention, but this is not developed within the provided text.

title: Fatale
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's conflicts. The film revolves around a double homicide, an attempted framing, and a corrupt cop's machinations. Characters explicitly discuss and plan violent acts, such as Derrick being told he could 'kill them first' and the detective stating 'They came at me, and I put 'em down.' The climax involves multiple murders and threats of violence, with characters resorting to physical force to achieve their goals, including framing others for crimes they didn't commit. Ultimately, the protagonist is exonerated, but only after navigating a web of violence and coercion.

title: After We Collided
justification: While the subtitles contain instances of aggression and conflict, force/violence is not structurally central to resolving the narrative's core issues. Characters engage in verbal altercations, and there are mentions of past violence (e.g., the assault Hardin witnessed as a child). However, the primary conflicts revolve around relationship dynamics, trust, and personal growth, which are addressed through dialogue and emotional confrontations rather than physical force. The narrative focuses on the characters' internal struggles and their attempts to navigate complex relationships, with the resolution primarily driven by emotional reconciliation and personal development.

title: The Lodge
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the film's core conflict. The narrative escalates from psychological tension to overt physical threats and violence, with characters resorting to aggressive actions to protect themselves and achieve their goals. Grace's increasingly erratic behavior culminates in violent acts, such as destroying property and threatening the children, which necessitates defensive actions. The climax involves a physical confrontation where survival depends on the ability to use force, as demonstrated by the children's attempts to defend themselves against Grace. The film's resolution hinges on the use of a gun, highlighting the dominance of force in resolving the conflict.

title: IP Man: The Finale
justification: Force/violence is a central theme in "Ip Man 4: The Finale." The narrative revolves around Ip Man's journey to America, where he encounters prejudice and conflict. Violence is consistently presented as a primary means of addressing these issues, such as when Ip Man confronts racist individuals at the school and later battles a Marine Gunnery Sergeant to defend the honor of Chinese martial arts. The film's climax involves a series of fights where physical prowess determines the outcome, reinforcing the idea that force is essential for resolving disputes and protecting one's community. Dialogue such as "In the face of injustice, I must stand up and fight" and the numerous fight scenes underscore the centrality of force in the narrative.

title: Half Brothers
justification: While the film does not heavily rely on violence as a primary means of resolving its central conflict, there are intermittent instances where force or the threat of force appears. For example, Asher's initial encounter with Renato involves him acting as a bully, and later, Asher punches Renato during an argument. Additionally, the brothers encounter rednecks who threaten them, and Asher gets beaten up. These instances suggest that force is present as a potential method of conflict resolution, but it is not the dominant or most effective approach. The narrative focuses more on emotional reconciliation and understanding.

title: The Personal History of David Copperfield
justification: While the narrative contains instances of physical force and coercion, they are not structurally central to resolving the core conflicts. Characters like Murdstone use physical discipline, and there's a boxing match, but these are isolated incidents. The primary conflicts revolve around social mobility, financial hardship, and personal relationships, which are resolved through a combination of personal growth, legal maneuvering, and social support rather than direct physical confrontation. The resolution of Uriah Heep's villainy relies on uncovering financial fraud, not physical violence. The tragic events in Yarmouth, while involving the storm's force, are more about loss and emotional reconciliation than a direct application of force to solve a problem.

title: The Wretched
justification: Force and violence are recurring elements in the narrative, though not always the primary solution. Ben assaults a sailing student at the marina after an argument, showcasing physical aggression as a response to conflict. The neighbor Abbie uses physical intimidation and implied threats of violence against Ben and others, escalating tension and driving the plot. Ben's father, Liam, physically restrains Ben during an argument, highlighting force as a means of control. The climax involves physical confrontations and struggles for survival against Abbie, where characters must fight to protect themselves and others, making violence a central component of the resolution.

title: The Rental
justification: Force/violence is central to the narrative's resolution. The film includes a character with a history of violence ("served jail time for nearly beating a guy to death"). The central conflict escalates to physical violence when Josh assaults Taylor after discovering he was filming them. This act of violence leads to Taylor's death, forcing the characters to consider covering it up. The dialogue explicitly mentions the possibility of "fucking kill[ing] him." The climax revolves around the characters' attempts to dispose of the body and the footage, highlighting the consequences of the initial violent act.

title: 2 Hearts
justification: The subtitles contain minimal reliance on force or violence as a means of resolving conflict. The narrative focuses on relationships, personal growth, and dealing with loss. There are no instances of characters explicitly endorsing violence or planning aggressive actions to solve problems. The conflicts are primarily internal or circumstantial, such as dealing with illness, career choices, and relationship challenges, which are resolved through dialogue, emotional support, and personal decisions rather than physical force. The only mention of force is when the father tells his son to 'put pressure on' during a soccer game.

title: Jay and Silent Bob Reboot
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this film. The narrative includes explicit threats and acts of violence, such as Millennium threatening to stab Jay and Silent Bob on her front lawn ("Either you take us to Hollywood or I stab you both to death on my own front fucking lawn!"). Operation Predator Editor involves physical coercion and assault. The climax involves a Russian agent attempting to execute Kevin Smith, leading to a chaotic fight with guns and physical altercations, including Jay physically attacking the agent and Iron Bob fighting off attackers. While the film also explores themes of family and reconciliation, these are often intertwined with or resolved through violent or aggressive actions.

title: Train to Busan Presents: Peninsula
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. The initial premise involves escaping zombies, necessitating violent encounters for survival ('We have to go. We have to go now, come on!'). Characters frequently resort to violence to protect themselves and others, as seen when the protagonist kills an infected person ('Here you go! Sir... Nice shot!'). The film's climax involves a large-scale battle with a rogue military unit, Unit 631, where force is the primary means of achieving their goals ('Just kill them all!'). The narrative also highlights the brutal reality of survival, where characters are forced to make difficult decisions involving violence to ensure their safety.

title: Promising Young Woman
justification: Force/violence is central to the narrative's resolution. The protagonist, Cassie, uses manipulation, threats, and ultimately physical violence to exact revenge on those who wronged her deceased friend, Nina. She confronts Dean Walker, threatening his daughter to get him to admit his role in dismissing Nina's case. She also confronts Ryan, threatening to release a compromising video unless he reveals the location of Al Monroe's bachelor party. The climax involves Cassie drugging and physically assaulting Al Monroe, intending to perform a non-consensual surgery on him as retribution for his actions against Nina. While the film explores themes of trauma and justice, the narrative relies heavily on Cassie's use of force and coercion to achieve her goals, making it a dominant engine of resolution.

title: Met Opera — Agrippina
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. Agrippina uses poison to remove Claudius and secure Nero's place as Emperor. Anicetus seeks revenge on Agrippina for her betrayal, indicating a violent response to perceived wrongs. Nero orders the assassination of his mother, Agrippina, and later sets Rome on fire, showcasing extreme violence as a means to achieve his desires and consolidate power. The narrative also mentions conspiracies and the pursuit of Nero by Galba's legions, further emphasizing the role of force in resolving political conflicts.

title: True to the Game 2: Gena’s Story
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this film. The narrative revolves around drug dealing, robberies, and revenge killings. Characters frequently resort to violence to achieve their goals, as seen when Saleem seeks to recover stolen drugs, leading to interrogations and threats. The film includes scenes of shootings, beatings, and planned attacks, such as the initial robbery and the subsequent pursuit of those responsible. The dialogue explicitly mentions killing as a means of settling scores, such as Saleem's determination to find and punish those who hijacked his shipment, and the revenge for Quadir's death. The characters' survival and success are directly linked to their capacity for violence and coercion.

title: The Assistant
justification: The subtitles primarily depict the inner workings of a talent agency, focusing on scheduling, client management, and office politics. There are a few instances that hint at potential coercion or aggressive behavior, such as blocking credit cards and yelling at subordinates, but these are isolated incidents. The dialogue does not explicitly endorse violence as a means of resolving conflicts, nor does it frame non-violent alternatives as weak. The narrative mainly revolves around professional interactions and personal relationships, with minimal reliance on force or violence to solve problems.

title: Love and Monsters
justification: Force and violence are central to the narrative's problem-solving, though not entirely dominant. The post-apocalyptic world necessitates constant combat against mutated creatures, as evidenced by the hunting parties and Joel's monster encounters. Dialogue such as "Well, suddenly you needed a shotgun. And sometimes even a tank" and the detailed descriptions of monster weaknesses in Joel's journal highlight the importance of force for survival. While Joel initially avoids violence, his character arc involves learning to fight and protect himself and others, culminating in his role in defeating the yacht captain and the crab monster. The film also explores non-violent solutions and emotional connections, but the constant threat of violent death shapes the characters' choices and actions.

title: Relic
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the core conflict. The narrative escalates to physical altercations as Edna's mental state deteriorates, culminating in violent confrontations between Edna, Kay, and Sam. Edna's actions, driven by her condition and perceived threats, directly lead to physical harm and danger, such as when she traps Jamie, injures Sam, and attempts to harm herself and others. The climax involves physical struggles and the need for coercive intervention to prevent further violence, highlighting force as a primary means of dealing with the escalating crisis.

title: The Tax Collector
justification: The subtitles strongly suggest that force and violence are central to resolving conflicts. Characters explicitly threaten each other with death and harm, such as Conejo's threats to the protagonist's family and the general talk of war and killing. The dialogue emphasizes the importance of power, protection from enemies, and the willingness to use violence to achieve goals. The phrase "For my family...I kill" encapsulates the idea that violence is a necessary and justifiable means of protecting loved ones and resolving disputes.

title: Becky
justification: Force/violence is the dominant engine of resolution in "Becky." The narrative revolves around escaped convicts who resort to extreme violence to achieve their goals, including murder and torture. The protagonist, Becky, initially a victim, progressively embraces violence as a means of survival and retribution. The film culminates in a series of brutal confrontations where Becky uses inventive and lethal methods to eliminate her adversaries, suggesting that only through violence can she protect herself and avenge her losses. Dialogue such as "You're about to find out what happens when you lie to me" and the graphic depiction of violent acts underscore the centrality of force in resolving the film's conflicts.

title: The Song of Names
justification: The subtitles suggest a historical context of violence and displacement, particularly referencing Warsaw and the loss of family members. The dialogue includes phrases like "Take him," indicating coercion, and the overall tone implies a situation where individuals are subject to external forces. However, the primary focus seems to be on remembrance and seeking community rather than actively engaging in or advocating for violence as a solution. The act of remembering the deceased suggests an attempt to cope with past violence, but the subtitles do not explicitly depict force as the main method of resolving present issues.

title: Break the Silence The Movie
justification: The subtitles primarily consist of the members of BTS watching a film of their past performances and reminiscing about those times. There is no explicit dialogue endorsing or planning violence to resolve disputes. Non-violent alternatives are not framed as weak, naive, or ineffective. Character progression is not tied to their willingness or ability to use force. Conflicts and climaxes do not structurally demand a violent or physically coercive resolution. Survival or justice does not depend strictly on the capacity to inflict harm. The only possible connection to force is the immense effort and energy they put into their performances, but this is not framed as a resolution to conflict.

title: All My Life
justification: The film's subtitles contain no instances of force or violence being used as a means of resolution. The narrative focuses on love, loss, and living in the moment, with characters facing health challenges and relationship issues. However, these challenges are addressed through emotional support, community, and personal growth, rather than physical force. The only mention of force is in the song lyrics "Hit me with your best shot," which is metaphorical and does not reflect actual violence within the narrative.

title: Met Opera: Wozzeck
justification: Force and violence are central to the narrative's resolution. Woyzeck's internal turmoil and jealousy culminate in the violent act of stabbing Marie to death, driven by her infidelity. The dialogue foreshadows this violence, with Woyzeck's increasing paranoia and the recurring motif of 'stab dead.' The narrative structure builds towards this violent climax, with Woyzeck's mental state deteriorating and his actions becoming increasingly erratic. The final scenes focus on the aftermath of the murder, highlighting the centrality of violence in resolving the conflict.

title: Cut Throat City
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this film. The narrative revolves around characters resorting to armed robbery and violent confrontations to escape poverty and exert control. Explicit dialogue, such as the opening threat to "burn your ass," and Cousin's brutal enforcement of debts through physical harm, highlight violence as a primary means of problem-solving. The characters' progression is directly tied to their willingness to engage in violent acts, culminating in a final robbery and shootout. While the film explores themes of community and survival, the dominant engine of resolution is undeniably force and violence.

title: A Hidden Life
justification: Force and violence are recurring themes, particularly in the context of war and political oppression. The film explores the moral conflict of participating in a war the protagonist doesn't believe in, where violence is the expected means of resolving international disputes. The Mayor's speech explicitly endorses violence against 'other races,' highlighting the aggressive coercion at the heart of the conflict. While the protagonist, Franz, resists violence, the narrative structure places him in a situation where his refusal to participate leads to his execution, implying that force is the ultimate arbiter, even if resisted. The film also shows the violence inflicted on those deemed enemies of the state, reinforcing the centrality of force in maintaining power.

title: Casino Royale
justification: The provided subtitles are primarily an audio commentary on the film *Casino Royale*, focusing on production details, casting choices, and technical aspects. While the commentary acknowledges the film's action sequences and stunts, it does not explicitly discuss the centrality of force or violence as a means of resolving the narrative's core conflicts. There are mentions of fight scenes, explosions, and dangerous stunts, but these are discussed in terms of their technical execution and realism rather than their narrative function as primary problem-solving tools. The commentary also highlights the film's focus on character development and complex relationships, suggesting that non-violent elements are also significant.

title: Death at a Funeral
justification: Force and violence are significantly present, though not dominant. The subtitles include a threat of violence ("If my dad's not In this coffin In one hour, than you have to take his place.") and physical altercations, such as the fight over the parking spot and the escalating chaos involving Oscar's drug-induced behavior. The narrative also features the blackmail plot, which involves the threat of revealing compromising photos unless a large sum of money is paid. The climax involves physical struggles, including attempts to restrain characters and prevent them from jumping off a roof, indicating that physical intervention is sometimes seen as a necessary solution.

title: American Hustle
justification: While the film revolves around deception and manipulation, physical force and violence are not central to resolving the core conflicts. There are a few instances of threatened or implied violence, such as when Carmine's associates intimidate Irving, or when Richie threatens Stoddard. However, these moments are not the primary drivers of the plot. The narrative focuses more on the characters' ability to con and outsmart each other, rather than resorting to physical aggression. The resolution of the plot hinges on strategic maneuvering and exposing corruption, not on violent confrontations.

title: The Age of Adaline
justification: The film's subtitles contain minimal reliance on force or violence to solve problems. While there are instances of characters being questioned by authorities, these situations are resolved through evasion and deception rather than physical confrontation. The narrative primarily focuses on Adaline's attempts to conceal her immortality and maintain a low profile, which involves changing identities and avoiding detection. The dialogue emphasizes her efforts to blend in and avoid suspicion, indicating that non-violent strategies are her primary means of navigating challenges.

title: Moana
justification: Force and violence are significantly present, though not dominant. The film's central conflict revolves around the theft of Te Fiti's heart, which unleashes a destructive force (Te Ka) that threatens the islands. Maui, initially presented as a warrior and trickster, uses his powers and fishhook for both benevolent and selfish purposes, including stealing the heart. Moana confronts Maui and later Te Ka, requiring her to navigate dangerous situations and ultimately leading to a confrontation with a lava monster. While the ultimate resolution involves restoring the heart with compassion, the journey there is fraught with peril and physical challenges, including battles with the Kakamora and Tamatoa.

title: The Revenant
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. The subtitles are replete with instances of characters resorting to violence for survival, revenge, and acquisition. The initial attack by the Ree results in significant loss of life and sets the stage for future violent encounters. Characters like Fitzgerald explicitly endorse violence, and the narrative culminates in Glass's pursuit of revenge, a quest driven by violence. The dialogue emphasizes the constant threat of attack and the necessity of defending oneself, making force a primary means of navigating the world.

title: Deepwater Horizon
justification: While the film does not depict interpersonal violence as a primary resolution method, the narrative heavily relies on the *potential* for catastrophic force and the characters' attempts to control it. The entire plot revolves around managing immense geological pressures, with the failure to do so resulting in a devastating explosion. The dialogue emphasizes the constant struggle against this force, such as the repeated references to 'taming the dinosaurs' (oil) and the Blowout Preventer. The climax involves a desperate attempt to contain the uncontrolled release of this force, making it the central conflict and resolution point, albeit a failed one. The film also shows the characters' willingness to use force to get what they want, such as when Mike and Jimmy threaten the BP executives.

title: The BFG
justification: Force and violence are significantly present, though not dominant. The central conflict revolves around man-eating giants who pose a direct threat, necessitating a violent solution. The BFG and Sophie's plan involves capturing the giants, which requires the use of military force. While the BFG initially avoids violence, the narrative ultimately relies on the army's intervention to subdue the giants and ensure the safety of children. The dialogue includes explicit mentions of giants eating children and the need to stop them, highlighting the centrality of force in resolving this threat.

title: Passengers
justification: Force and violence are moderately salient in "Passengers." While the initial conflict stems from a mechanical malfunction, the narrative escalates to include physical threats and the necessity of violence to ensure survival. Jim's initial act of waking Aurora is a form of coercion, though not physically violent, it forces her into a situation against her will. Later, the characters face a critical situation where they must physically venture into a dangerous environment to repair the ship, culminating in Jim's sacrifice to vent the reactor. The dialogue emphasizes the urgency and the lack of non-violent alternatives, making force a significant, though not dominant, method of resolution.

title: Hell or High Water
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the film's core conflict. The narrative revolves around bank robberies, where the protagonists explicitly use guns and threats to steal money. Dialogue such as "Open the drawer! Open the motherfucking drawer!" and scenes depicting shootouts with law enforcement and civilians highlight the reliance on force. The film's climax involves a violent confrontation where one of the protagonists is killed, underscoring the narrative's dependence on force as a primary means of conflict resolution. The justification for the violence is economic desperation, but the method is consistently violent.

title: The Forest
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's core conflict. The protagonist, Sara, enters a suicide forest to find her twin sister, Jess. While initially driven by a desire to rescue Jess, the narrative escalates to include physical confrontations and the threat of violence. Aiden's deception and subsequent attack on Sara, Sara's violent confrontation with the perceived antagonist, and the eventual physical struggle with Jess, who is possessed or mentally unstable, all highlight the centrality of force. The climax involves physical struggles and the need to inflict harm for survival, making force a dominant engine of resolution.

title: Fences
justification: While the play explores themes of racial injustice and personal struggles, force/violence is not structurally central to resolving the narrative's core conflicts. Troy's aggressive personality and past experiences with physical labor and racial discrimination inform his interactions, but dialogue primarily revolves around verbal disputes, familial disagreements, and personal ambitions rather than physical confrontations. Troy's wrestling match with death is metaphorical, and his physical altercation with Cory is a culmination of long-standing emotional tensions, not a primary means of problem-solving. The narrative focuses more on the characters' internal struggles and relationships than on the application of force to overcome obstacles, though the threat of force is present.

title: Wonder Woman
justification: Force/violence is central to resolving the narrative. Diana's journey is predicated on her belief that Ares is corrupting mankind and that defeating him will end the war. Dialogue explicitly frames violence as necessary to combat Ares' influence, with Diana stating, "Stopping the God of War is our foreordinance." Her training as an Amazon is geared towards combat, and her primary method of problem-solving involves physical confrontation, as seen in her actions on the battlefield and her willingness to fight Ludendorff/Ares. While the film also explores themes of love and choice, the core conflict and its resolution are driven by violent acts and the capacity to inflict harm.

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. The Guardians are hired to protect valuable batteries, and their success is measured by their ability to defeat a large beast, which Drax attempts to do by cutting his way through it from the inside. Rocket steals batteries, leading to a space battle with the Sovereign, who explicitly order their fleet to "fire with the intent to kill." Characters like Nebula and Taserface are driven by revenge and a desire to inflict harm, and the climax involves a large-scale battle against Ego, requiring the Guardians to destroy him to save the universe.

title: It
justification: Force and violence are central to the narrative's resolution. The film revolves around a group of children confronting a supernatural entity that terrorizes their town. The primary method of dealing with this entity involves physical confrontation and attempts to harm or destroy it, as seen in the rock fight with Bowers' gang and the final confrontation with Pennywise. Dialogue such as "Kill It, Bill!" and scenes of characters physically fighting the monster demonstrate the reliance on force. While fear and unity are also important themes, the climax hinges on the Losers' Club's ability to physically overcome Pennywise, making force a dominant engine of resolution.

title: Despicable Me 3
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. The primary antagonist, Bratt, uses violence and threats of violence to achieve his goals, requiring Gru and Lucy to use force to stop him. Gru's brother, Dru, also embraces villainy and engages in violent acts, indicating a family tradition of using force. The climax involves a dance fight and physical confrontation, highlighting the importance of physical prowess in resolving the conflict. Dialogue such as "Let's get physical" and the constant need to stop Bratt's violent plans demonstrate the salience of force as a resolution method.

title: The Fate of the Furious
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this film. The narrative revolves around Dom being blackmailed into working for Cipher, a cyberterrorist, who uses threats of violence against his son and Elena to coerce him. The team frequently resorts to aggressive tactics, including car chases, explosions, and hand-to-hand combat, to stop Cipher's plans. The film culminates in a series of violent confrontations, including a submarine chase and a showdown on an ice field, where the team uses their driving skills and weaponry to disable Cipher's forces and prevent a nuclear attack. The dialogue is filled with threats and plans for violent action, such as "Neutralize their shooters, and then move on to our objective" and "You're gonna want to work for me. You're gonna betray your brothers, abandon your code, and shatter your family."

title: Justice League
justification: Force/violence is a central theme in this narrative. The plot revolves around an impending alien invasion, with characters preparing for and engaging in combat. Dialogue explicitly mentions the need for "warriors" and "an alliance to defend ourselves." The film culminates in a large-scale battle against Steppenwolf and his Parademons, where physical force is the primary means of resolving the conflict. The heroes' success depends on their ability to fight and inflict harm, making force a dominant engine of resolution.

title: Dunkirk
justification: Force and violence are central to the narrative of Dunkirk. The entire premise revolves around extracting soldiers from a warzone where they face constant aerial bombardment and naval attacks. Dialogue such as "The enemy had something to say about it," regarding why Calais couldn't be used for evacuation, and the repeated scenes of dogfights and bombings, highlight the ever-present threat of violence. The film's climax involves a desperate struggle for survival against enemy attacks, with characters making difficult choices, including sacrificing one person to save others, demonstrating how force dictates their actions and resolutions.

title: The Lego Batman Movie
justification: Force is a recurring method for resolution, sharing centrality with other approaches. Batman frequently resorts to physical violence to subdue villains, as seen in his initial fight with the assembled villains at the energy plant and his later confrontations. The narrative also presents non-violent approaches, such as Commissioner Gordon's emphasis on statistics and compassion, and the Joker's initial surrender, which are ultimately subverted or proven ineffective. The climax involves a large-scale battle where physical force is essential to saving Gotham, although teamwork and emotional connection are also highlighted as crucial elements. The film balances the necessity of force with the importance of relationships and community, suggesting that while violence is a tool, it is not the only or ideal solution.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. Characters frequently resort to aggressive actions, such as sword fights, cannon fire, and physical coercion, to overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. For example, Salazar and his crew use violence to hunt Jack Sparrow, while Barbossa uses threats to get information. The film's climax involves a physical struggle to break the Trident, which is essential for resolving the curses. The dialogue emphasizes the importance of strength and aggression in a world filled with pirates and supernatural threats, making force a primary means of survival and achieving objectives.

title: Annabelle: Creation
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's core conflict. The film revolves around a demonic entity that uses violence and manipulation to achieve its goals, culminating in multiple deaths and physical assaults. Characters are either victims of violence (Janice's physical attacks, Sister Charlotte's death) or actively engaged in violent acts to survive (Linda destroying the doll, attempts to escape the demon). The climax involves a direct confrontation with the demonic entity, where physical force is the only means of defense, even if ultimately ineffective. The narrative strongly suggests that the characters' survival depends on their ability to recognize and combat the violent threat, making force a dominant engine of resolution.

title: Daddy’s Home 2
justification: While the film primarily focuses on family dynamics and emotional resolutions, force and violence appear intermittently. There are instances of physical aggression, such as the snowball fight and the near-wrestling match between Kurt and Dusty, but these are played for comedic effect and ultimately resolved through apologies and reconciliation. The daughter accidentally shooting her grandfather while hunting is a violent act, but it leads to emotional bonding rather than further conflict. The film does not suggest that violence is the primary or most effective way to solve problems, but it is present as a disruptive element that characters must overcome.

title: Tyler Perry’s Boo 2! A Madea Halloween
justification: Force and violence are central to the resolution of conflicts in this film. The narrative revolves around characters facing threats, both real and perceived, that often lead to aggressive responses. Madea and Joe frequently advocate for physical violence as a solution to problems, such as Joe suggesting Brian "beat his ass!" when Tiffany's stepfather is present. The climax involves characters being chased by a chainsaw-wielding killer, and Madea ultimately confronts the threat with her own brand of aggressive, albeit comedic, force. The film also portrays characters resorting to violence to protect themselves and others, highlighting the importance of physical strength and aggression in surviving the night's events.

title: Patriots Day
justification: Force and violence are central to the narrative's resolution. The film revolves around the Boston Marathon bombing and the subsequent manhunt for the perpetrators. The dialogue explicitly details the planning and execution of violent acts, such as the bombing itself ("Those are bombs, Captain!") and the shootout with police ("Shots fired! Shots fired!"). Non-violent alternatives are largely absent, and the narrative emphasizes the necessity of using force to apprehend the suspects and prevent further harm. The climax involves a violent confrontation, and the resolution depends on the successful application of force by law enforcement.

title: Black Panther
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in "Black Panther." The narrative revolves around challenges for the throne, which are settled through ritual combat, where yielding or death determines the victor. The film also highlights the use of force to protect Wakanda's vibranium and maintain its secrecy, as seen in the multiple fight scenes. Killmonger's plan to arm oppressed people with vibranium weapons to overthrow existing power structures further emphasizes force as a means of resolution. T'Challa ultimately defeats Killmonger through combat, reclaiming the throne and preventing a global conflict fueled by Wakandan weaponry, though he is clearly conflicted about the role of violence.

title: Avengers: Infinity War
justification: Force and violence are overwhelmingly central to resolving the narrative. The film revolves around Thanos's quest to acquire the Infinity Stones and use them to eliminate half of all life in the universe, a goal achieved through immense violence and destruction. The heroes' primary objective is to stop him, which they attempt to do through direct physical confrontation and strategic use of their powers. Dialogue such as "You're about to die at the hands of the Children of Thanos" and the numerous battle sequences demonstrate the film's reliance on force as the primary means of conflict resolution. The climax involves a massive battle in Wakanda, and the film concludes with Thanos succeeding in his violent plan, highlighting the dominance of force in the narrative.

title: A Star is Born
justification: While not a constant presence, force and violence are central to the narrative's resolution. The film does not explicitly endorse violence as a solution, but it is a recurring element, particularly in relation to Jack's self-destructive behavior. Jack's physical altercation in the cop bar after a fan harasses Ally demonstrates his willingness to use force, though it is framed as protective. More significantly, Jack's internal struggles and substance abuse culminate in his suicide, a violent act that, while not directly solving a problem for others, is presented as his only way out of his personal turmoil. The narrative implies that his inability to cope non-violently leads to this tragic end.

title: The Meg
justification: Force/violence is central to resolving the narrative's core conflict. The film revolves around confronting and ultimately killing megalodons, prehistoric sharks, to protect human lives. Dialogue emphasizes the necessity of lethal force, such as the discussion of injecting the meg with a lethal substance: "A killer whale is knocked out with 10 CCs. Dead with 20. What do you think? I think we use the whole damn bottle." The narrative climaxes with characters actively hunting and deploying explosives against the sharks, highlighting force as the primary means of problem-solving. The film's resolution depends on the characters' ability to inflict harm on the megalodons, solidifying force as a dominant theme.

title: Smallfoot
justification: While the film emphasizes curiosity, understanding, and communication, force and violence are present as potential, though not dominant, methods of resolution. The Stonekeeper initially uses banishment as a coercive tool to control Migo and maintain the status quo. The film also depicts the yetis' historical fear of humans, stemming from violent encounters, which motivates their isolationist society. Additionally, Percy's initial plan involves capturing a yeti, implying a forceful approach, and he later uses a tranquilizer gun, though ultimately for self-defense. These instances suggest that force is a relevant, but not central, element in the narrative's problem-solving.

title: The Post
justification: The film's subtitles contain limited direct endorsements of violence as a solution, but the context of the Vietnam War inherently involves force. Characters discuss military operations ("Fire mission. Grid 298471") and casualties, indicating the ongoing conflict. However, the dialogue focuses more on political decisions, media coverage, and the ethical dilemmas surrounding the war rather than explicitly advocating for violence. The narrative's central conflict revolves around the publication of the Pentagon Papers, a non-violent act of revealing information, which suggests that truth and transparency are presented as alternative means of addressing the problems caused by the war.

title: Game Night
justification: Force and violence are extremely central to resolving the narrative's core conflicts. The plot escalates from a seemingly harmless murder mystery game into a real-life criminal conspiracy involving smuggling, black market dealings, and dangerous felons. Characters are repeatedly threatened with violence, shot, and forced to engage in physical altercations to survive. The climax involves a high-stakes confrontation on a plane, where characters resort to physical force and even death to protect themselves and others. The narrative consistently presents violence as the primary means of dealing with escalating threats, with characters like Max and Annie ultimately embracing violent solutions to overcome seemingly insurmountable odds.

title: Instant Family
justification: While the film primarily focuses on the emotional and social challenges of foster care and adoption, force/violence is present, albeit not central to resolving the narrative's core conflicts. There are instances of physical aggression, such as Lita's violent outbursts (throwing a glass, wielding a knife) and Pete's physical confrontation with Charlie (though mistaken identity). These moments create tension and highlight the difficulties the family faces, but they are not the primary drivers of the plot. The narrative emphasizes communication, empathy, and perseverance as the main tools for overcoming obstacles, rather than relying on force.

title: Maze Runner: The Death Cure
justification: Force and violence are overwhelmingly central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. The film opens with a violent train heist ("Brenda, we're coming up behind. Keep 'em busy.") and continues with constant fighting, shooting, and explosions. Characters repeatedly use weapons and physical force to overcome obstacles and enemies. The narrative climaxes with a large-scale battle for control of the city, and the protagonists' survival depends on their ability to fight and inflict harm. Even the attempts to find a cure are framed as a struggle against WICKED, requiring aggressive action and combat.

title: Red Sparrow
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this film. Characters are coerced, tortured, and killed to obtain information or eliminate threats. Dominika is forced into becoming a 'Sparrow,' where she learns to use seduction and manipulation as weapons. The dialogue explicitly mentions the use of violence, such as when Volontov threatens to have someone arrested for assault or when the characters discuss the torture and murder of Marta. The narrative revolves around espionage, betrayal, and the constant threat of physical harm, making force a primary driver of the plot.

title: Breaking In
justification: Force/violence is the dominant engine of resolution. The narrative revolves around a home invasion where the protagonists are forced to defend themselves against violent criminals. The dialogue is replete with threats and acts of violence, such as the intruders' plans to kill the family and the mother's desperate measures to protect her children. The climax involves a physical confrontation where the mother uses force to eliminate the intruders, highlighting violence as the ultimate means of survival and resolution. The entire plot hinges on the application of force, making it the central method for resolving the conflict.

title: 12 Strong
justification: Force and violence are overwhelmingly central to resolving the narrative's core conflict. The film explicitly focuses on a Special Forces team tasked with using military force to combat the Taliban in Afghanistan following the 9/11 attacks. Dialogue consistently emphasizes the necessity of violent action, with characters planning and executing airstrikes and ground assaults. The narrative revolves around the team's ability to inflict harm on the enemy, with survival and mission success directly tied to their capacity for violence. The climax involves a major battle where the team's use of force is crucial for achieving their objectives, solidifying force/violence as the dominant engine of resolution.

title: First Man
justification: The subtitles primarily focus on the technical and emotional aspects of space exploration, with minimal emphasis on force or violence as a means of resolving conflict. The narrative centers on the challenges and triumphs of the space program, the personal sacrifices of the astronauts and their families, and the global impact of the Moon landing. While there are mentions of the Cold War space race with the Soviets, this competition is framed more as a technological and ideological contest rather than a violent one. The dialogue does not explicitly endorse or plan violence, nor does it frame non-violent alternatives as weak or ineffective. The narrative's conflicts are resolved through engineering, problem-solving, and perseverance, not through force.

title: Acrimony
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's core conflicts. The protagonist, Melinda, frequently resorts to aggression and physical altercations when confronted with betrayal and emotional distress. This is evident in her initial violent outburst towards Robert and his mistress, resulting in physical harm and legal consequences. Later, her rage escalates to stalking, harassment, and ultimately, a violent confrontation on a yacht, culminating in attempted murder. The narrative structure emphasizes these violent acts as expressions of Melinda's unresolved anger and the destructive consequences of her inability to cope with betrayal non-violently, making force a dominant engine of resolution.

title: Sherlock Gnomes
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the core conflict. The narrative revolves around Sherlock Gnomes' battles with Moriarty, where the threat of gnomes being 'smashed' (destroyed) drives the plot. Sherlock's methods often involve physical confrontations, and the climax involves a direct physical showdown to prevent Moriarty from crushing all the gnomes. Dialogue such as 'I'll stop you until the day I die' and the constant threat of physical harm highlight the centrality of force in this conflict. The resolution depends on Sherlock's ability to physically defeat Moriarty and prevent the violent destruction of the gnomes.

title: Truth or Dare
justification: Force and violence are central to the narrative's resolution. The film revolves around a supernatural game of Truth or Dare where characters are compelled to either truthfully answer a question or complete a dare, with refusal resulting in death. This is explicitly stated multiple times, such as when Carter explains, "Tell the truth or you die. Do the dare or you die. Refuse to play and..." and when Olivia says, "Ronnie didn't do his dare, and now he's dead!" The characters' survival depends on their willingness to engage in increasingly dangerous and violent acts, or to reveal damaging truths, highlighting force and coercion as the primary drivers of the plot. The climax involves a ritual to trap the demon, requiring a violent act of self-mutilation, further solidifying the theme's centrality.

title: Paddington 2
justification: While the film emphasizes kindness and community, force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's core conflict. Paddington is wrongly imprisoned and must navigate a violent prison environment, where his survival depends on gaining the protection of the prison's toughest inmate, Knuckles, through his culinary skills. The film's climax involves a physical confrontation on a moving train, where characters engage in direct combat to retrieve the stolen pop-up book and exonerate Paddington. The narrative also features Phoenix Buchanan, who uses physical force and coercion to steal the book and evade capture, highlighting the importance of physical prowess in achieving his goals.

title: Peppermint
justification: Force/violence is the dominant engine of resolution in this film. The narrative revolves around Riley North's transformation into a vigilante after her family is murdered. The subtitles explicitly show her using violence to exact revenge on those responsible, including drug dealers, corrupt officials, and gang members. Dialogue such as "I'm gonna kill them" and scenes depicting executions and bombings demonstrate the centrality of force. The film's climax involves a large-scale shootout, further emphasizing violence as the primary means of achieving justice and resolving conflict.

title: Annihilation
justification: Force and violence are recurring elements in the narrative, though not always the primary solution. The characters are armed and prepared for combat, as evidenced by their military backgrounds and discussions of weapons. The dialogue reveals that previous expeditions faced violent ends, either through external threats or internal conflict ("One, something kills them. Two, they go crazy and kill each other."). The team encounters and combats mutated creatures, requiring them to use force for survival (e.g., the alligator attack, the bear attack). However, the film also emphasizes scientific investigation and understanding, suggesting a balance between force and knowledge as means of navigating the Shimmer.

title: Isle of Dogs
justification: Force and violence are recurring elements in the narrative, though not the sole drivers of resolution. The film opens with a historical account of a war between dogs and cats, establishing a precedent for violent conflict. The present-day narrative includes dog-catchers who use force to capture and deport dogs, and there are mentions of dogs being violently destroyed. Characters like Chief are known for their fighting abilities, and there are instances of dogs attacking each other. However, the central conflict is ultimately resolved through non-violent means, such as Atari's haiku and the revelation of the Dog-Flu cure, which sway public opinion and lead to political change.

title: Adrift
justification: The film primarily focuses on survival and resilience in the face of a natural disaster. While the characters face life-threatening situations, the narrative emphasizes resourcefulness, problem-solving, and emotional endurance rather than physical force or violence. The dialogue centers on navigation, repair, and rationing, with minimal emphasis on aggressive conflict. The storm itself is the primary antagonist, and the characters' response is largely defensive and reactive, not involving direct confrontation or violence. The film's resolution depends on Tami's ability to navigate and survive, not on her capacity to inflict harm.

title: Robin Hood
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. The film depicts war, theft, and rebellion, all heavily reliant on physical force. Characters like Robin Hood and Gisbourne frequently resort to violence to achieve their goals, whether it's stealing from the rich or enforcing the Sheriff's oppressive rule. The narrative repeatedly showcases violent acts as necessary for survival and achieving justice, such as the raid on the mines and the final confrontation with the Sheriff. The dialogue emphasizes the inevitability of violence, with characters like John training Robin to fight and survive, highlighting that 'This war will be fought up close.'

title: Super Troopers 2
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this film. The narrative involves police officers and Canadian Mounties engaging in physical altercations, gunfights, and acts of sabotage against each other. Dialogue such as "Suck these fucking bullets, bitch!" and the repeated use of firearms highlight the reliance on violence. The plot escalates from pranks and insults to kidnapping, attempted murder, and ultimately a violent showdown at a sawmill, where characters resort to gunfire and physical combat to resolve their disputes, indicating that force is a primary means of problem-solving.

title: Slender Man
justification: Force and violence are central to the narrative's resolution. The film revolves around the characters' confrontation with the Slender Man, a supernatural entity that inflicts harm and drives people to madness or disappearance. The characters attempt to 'unveil themselves' by offering sacrifices, indicating a belief that appeasing the entity through a form of coerced exchange can resolve their problems. The climax involves characters being physically and mentally tormented, with the ultimate 'resolution' involving a character offering herself to the Slender Man to save her sister, highlighting the dominance of force and sacrifice in the narrative's problem-solving approach. The dialogue explicitly mentions the Slender Man's ability to 'take' people, and the characters' actions are driven by fear of his power.

title: Toy Story 4
justification: While the film contains elements of conflict and danger, force/violence is not structurally central to resolving the narrative's core issues. The toys face obstacles, such as escaping the antique store and rescuing Forky, but these are primarily overcome through cleverness, teamwork, and emotional appeals rather than physical force. There are instances of characters using physical actions, such as Buzz attacking the carnival prizes, but these are more comedic and serve to advance the plot rather than being the primary means of resolution. The central conflict revolves around Woody's struggle to accept change and Bonnie's need for Forky, which are resolved through emotional growth and understanding, not violence.

title: Frozen II
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the film's core conflicts. The initial conflict arises from a 'brutal battle' between Arendelle and the Northuldra, sparked by perceived aggression and leading to the spirits' wrath. The narrative progresses with the threat of the awakened spirits and the need to 'be prepared for whatever danger it may bring.' Elsa's journey involves confronting and potentially subduing these powerful spirits, while Anna's actions include physically confronting Earth Giants and ultimately destroying the dam, an act of significant force with potentially devastating consequences. The film's climax hinges on Elsa's ability to control her powers and navigate the dangers of Ahtohallan, implying that her strength and magical abilities are crucial for resolving the past and securing the future.

title: Captain Marvel
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's conflicts. The film revolves around a war between the Kree and the Skrulls, with both sides engaging in violent acts. Vers/Carol's initial training and purpose are centered on being a Kree warrior, emphasizing combat skills and suppressing emotions. The narrative progresses through battles, ambushes, and displays of power, with characters frequently resorting to physical force to overcome obstacles. The climax involves a direct confrontation with the Kree, where Carol uses her powers to defeat them and ultimately decides to end the war, indicating that force is a primary means of addressing the central conflict.

title: Spider-Man: Far From Home
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's conflicts. The film revolves around battles with 'Elementals' and later, Mysterio's illusions, both requiring physical confrontation. Characters like Spider-Man and Mysterio are defined by their capacity to inflict harm or defend against it. Dialogue such as "We have one mission: kill it" and scenes depicting drone strikes and energy blasts highlight the reliance on force. The climax involves a large-scale battle in London, where Spider-Man must use his powers to defeat Mysterio and his drones, emphasizing that the central conflict is resolved through physical force.

title: Aladdin
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. Jafar explicitly states his belief in power through coercion, saying he had to do many things to get the power that he has, including burying bodies. Aladdin's journey involves escaping guards, and Jafar's power grab relies on aggressive coercion and magical force. The climax involves Jafar using his sorcery to dominate Agrabah, and Aladdin must outsmart him to restore order, ultimately trapping Jafar in a lamp.

title: Us
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the film's core conflict. The narrative establishes a clear threat in the form of the Tethered, doppelgangers who seek to replace their surface-dwelling counterparts through violent means. The dialogue explicitly frames the conflict as a fight for survival, with Adelaide stating, "They won't stop until they kill us or we kill them." Characters like Gabe attempt to use physical force to defend their property, and Zora's "kill count" becomes a morbid metric of success. The climax involves a violent confrontation between Adelaide and her Tethered double, Red, where only one can survive, solidifying force as the ultimate means of resolution.

title: Pokémon: Detective Pikachu
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the film's core conflicts. The narrative repeatedly emphasizes physical conflict, experimentation on Pokemon to enhance their power, and the use of a mind-altering gas (R) to control Pokemon and humans. The climax involves a city-wide threat where Pokemon are forced to merge with humans, leading to widespread chaos and requiring violent intervention. Characters like Roger Clifford and Howard Clifford (possessed by Mewtwo) explicitly use force and coercion to achieve their goals, highlighting the film's reliance on physical power as a means of control and resolution. The protagonist, Tim, must engage in Pokemon battles and confront violent threats to uncover the truth and save his father.

title: Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in this narrative. The opening advertisement for "Bounty Law" explicitly states that Jake Cahill often kills his targets rather than bringing them in alive, highlighting violence as a primary method. Rick Dalton's roles often involve fight scenes where he loses, but his character Caleb in "Lancer" uses aggressive tactics, including throwing a child, to intimidate others. Cliff Booth's backstory includes killing his wife, and he engages in a physical contest with Bruce Lee, further emphasizing violence. The climax involves a home invasion by the Manson family, which is violently thwarted by Cliff and Rick, showcasing force as the ultimate resolution to the threat.

title: Shazam!
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the film's conflicts. The primary antagonist, Dr. Sivana, explicitly uses violence to obtain power and seeks to eliminate the protagonist. The Seven Deadly Sins, released by Sivana, cause widespread destruction and necessitate violent confrontation. The protagonist, Billy Batson, initially uses his powers for personal gain but eventually learns to use them to protect his foster family and the city, engaging in physical battles with Sivana and the Sins. The narrative culminates in a large-scale battle where force is the primary means of defeating the villains, with the protagonist and his foster siblings using their powers to fight and subdue the Sins.

title: Dumbo
justification: Force and violence are moderately salient in "Dumbo." While the film doesn't explicitly endorse violence as the *ideal* solution, it's a recurring element in resolving conflicts and maintaining order. For example, Rufus is violent towards Mrs. Jumbo, and the crowd turns violent against Dumbo during his performance, shouting insults and throwing things. Vandevere orders Mrs. Jumbo to be killed, and the security guards use force to control the crowds and recapture Dumbo. The climax involves a fire and chaotic escape, where characters must physically fight to survive and protect Dumbo. While the film also emphasizes themes of family and acceptance, force is consistently present as a means of control and a response to perceived threats.

title: Glass
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving the narrative's conflicts. The film revolves around individuals with superhuman abilities, and their confrontations often involve physical altercations. Characters like The Beast and David Dunn (Overseer) directly engage in violent acts, and the narrative emphasizes their physical strength and fighting abilities. The climax involves a showdown where these abilities are pitted against each other, and the resolution hinges on physical dominance. The dialogue also includes threats and plans for violence, such as the intention to blow up a building, further highlighting the centrality of force.

title: The Upside
justification: While not dominant, force and coercion appear intermittently as problem-solving tools. The initial police encounter involves physical restraint and the threat of arrest, though it is based on a misunderstanding. Dell's past as a thief and his concealed weapon charge are mentioned, suggesting a history of using force or coercion. Latrice threatens Dell with legal action ('reporting you') regarding child support. Dell's physical removal from Latrice's apartment ('Get out!') also implies a potential for conflict, though it doesn't escalate. These instances suggest force is a background element, but not the primary driver of the narrative's resolution.

title: Hustlers
justification: Force and violence are recurring, relevant, but not dominant methods for resolving conflict in "Hustlers." While the film primarily focuses on economic exploitation and manipulation, the threat and occasional use of physical force are present. Ramona's line, "You either gotta stand in the corner or get in the ring," suggests a willingness to engage in aggressive tactics. The film also depicts instances where characters resort to physical coercion, such as when Ramona confronts Destiny about the phone, stating, "Gimme that fucking phone. Ungrateful little bitch." The presence of bouncers and the occasional need for physical intervention to control unruly clients further underscore the role of force, though it is not the primary driver of the narrative.

title: Alita: Battle Angel
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in Alita: Battle Angel. The narrative repeatedly emphasizes the necessity of combat skills for survival and achieving goals. Alita's identity as a URM Berserker, a highly advanced cyborg weapon, structurally ties her character arc to violence. Dialogue such as "I'm gonna rip her in half" and scenes of Motorball, a violent sport, further highlight the prevalence of force. The film's climax involves Alita embracing her warrior identity to confront Nova, indicating that force is the primary means to address the central conflict.

title: Good Boys
justification: Force and violence are recurring, though not dominant, methods for resolving conflict. The narrative includes instances where characters resort to physical aggression or threats to achieve their goals. For example, the Scooter Squad's bullying involves intimidation and the threat of physical harm. The protagonists also engage in physical altercations, such as when they confront the girls to retrieve the drone, and when Max fights the college student in the drug den. While the narrative also explores non-violent solutions, the presence and impact of force contribute to its structural relevance.

title: Yesterday
justification: The subtitles contain almost no instances of force or violence being used to resolve conflict. The narrative focuses on Jack's musical journey and his relationships. The closest instance is when Rocky gets fired for accidentally spilling tea on Michael, but this is a minor event and doesn't drive the plot. The narrative primarily revolves around Jack's struggle with fame, authenticity, and his feelings for Ellie, all of which are resolved through dialogue, self-reflection, and ultimately, honesty.

title: Tyler Perry’s A Madea Family Funeral
justification: While the film primarily revolves around family drama and comedic situations, force/violence appears intermittently. Uncle Heathrow threatens physical violence multiple times, such as when he says he'll kick someone in the nuts with his cane or fist: "Touch this and see if you don't get kicked in the nut." Madea also frequently resorts to threats and physical altercations, like when she hits Hattie for speaking out of turn. However, these instances are more comedic and don't drive the central narrative, which focuses on relationships and personal growth. The film's conflicts are resolved through dialogue and emotional breakthroughs rather than physical force.

title: Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark
justification: Force and violence are central to resolving conflicts in "Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark." The narrative repeatedly demonstrates that characters resort to physical aggression and coercion to solve problems, such as Tommy's bullying behavior and the climactic confrontation with Sarah Bellows. Non-violent solutions are largely absent or ineffective, as seen in the characters' inability to reason with or escape the supernatural threats without resorting to physical struggle.
